headline: Live high, train low raised athletes' VO2max by about 2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; other hypoxic methods did not
question: Do intermittent hypoxic methods raise maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) more than the same training in normal air, and does it matter whether the people are athletes?
design: A systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression of controlled studies in healthy people, from PubMed, EMBASE and Web of Science (5,244 records screened, 62 studies included). In all there were 1,332 participants: 610 athletes and 722 non-athletes (baseline VO2max above 60 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ counted as athlete). Three methods were compared (10 LHTL, 45 LLTH and 11 PHC studies; three studies ran two methods) with control: live-high train-low (LHTL, living at altitude or in a hypoxic room and training at low altitude), live-low train-high (LLTH, training in thin air, living at sea level) and passive hypoxic conditioning (PHC, resting in hypoxia, training in normal air). Study risk of bias was rated with RoB2; no GRADE certainty rating was made, and publication bias with funnel plots and the Egger test.
findings:
Athletes: LHTL raised VO2max more than control (mean difference 2.17 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, 95% CI 0.77 to 3.56). LLTH (0.89, CI −0.27 to 2.05) and PHC (−1.07, CI −3.51 to 1.37) did not.

Non-athletes: LLTH (1.70, CI 0.85 to 2.54) and PHC (2.26, CI 1.00 to 3.52) raised VO2max; LHTL did not clearly (3.10, CI −0.23 to 6.43, from a single study).

Meta-regression linked the size of the change to how severe the hypoxia was (in LLTH), how long each daily exposure lasted and how often it was repeated; it found no such factor for LHTL. The authors call all the gains "relatively small". The Egger test showed no sign of publication bias (p = 0.67).
limits: Few studies blinded participants: none of the 10 LHTL studies, 32% of LLTH and 25% of PHC studies. RoB2 rated most studies "some concerns" or "high risk", and the authors say placebo effects are likely, especially for LHTL, where people know they are living at altitude. The athlete LHTL result rests on about nine unblinded studies, and only four PHC studies involved athletes. Studies were mostly of young men (81% men in LLTH); the authors say the effect in women and older people is unknown. Athlete status was partly judged from VO2max (above 60 counted as athlete). Pooling by method mixes different training types. The paper reports no heterogeneity statistic (I²) in its text or figure captions and no GRADE rating, so how consistent the studies were cannot be judged; with high risk of bias and no blinding, certainty would likely rate low. The abstract says standardised mean differences were calculated, but all results are raw mean differences in mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. VO2max is not race performance: the authors note that LLTH may help sport performance without moving VO2max. The work had no specific funding and the authors report no conflicts of interest; the first author held a European Respiratory Society fellowship.
meaning: The lessons on what limits VO2max and how trainable it is (vo2-trainability, vo2-limits) teach that VO2max in trained athletes moves only a little, and that the response differs between people. This review fits: gains of about 2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ are small next to the 60+ already in the athletes, and in athletes the benefit appears only for the live-high method, which works partly through blood volume and haemoglobin mass (o2-hb-mass). The study is also a lesson in appraisal (ev-pyramid): a meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it pools, and altitude studies are hard to blind. The altitude module (t6-altitude) is not written yet.

variants.stem: A cyclist with a VO2max of 72 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ wants the method in the 2026 hypoxic-training meta-analysis that raised athletes' VO2max. Which one?

options.text: Live high, train low, sleeping at altitude and training near sea level
options.why: Right: LHTL raised athletes' VO2max by 2.17 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (95% CI 0.77 to 3.56) over control.

options.text: Live low, train high, with the hard sessions done in thin air
options.why: LLTH did not raise athletes' VO2max significantly (0.89, CI −0.27 to 2.05).

options.text: Passive hypoxic conditioning, resting in thin air between sessions
options.why: PHC did not help athletes (−1.07, CI −3.51 to 1.37), and only four athlete studies existed.

options.text: Whichever method uses the thinnest air, since severity drove gains
options.why: Severity was linked to gains in LLTH, not LHTL, and in athletes only LHTL beat control.

variants.stem: A triathlete (VO2max 68 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) can only do hard sessions in a hypoxic chamber at his club. What does the 2026 meta-analysis suggest for his VO2max?

options.text: Probably little gain; live-low train-high was not significant in athletes
options.why: Right: LLTH gave 0.89 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ in athletes with a CI from −0.27 to 2.05, which includes no effect.

options.text: A clear gain of about 2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, as with live-high train-low
options.why: That figure belongs to LHTL, a different method.

options.text: A clear loss, since hypoxic training cuts training quality
options.why: The pooled effect was slightly positive but not significant, not negative.

options.text: A larger gain than a non-athlete would get
options.why: Non-athletes gained more from LLTH (1.70, CI 0.85 to 2.54) and it was significant.

variants.stem: In the 2026 hypoxic-training meta-analysis, passive hypoxic conditioning raised VO2max in non-athletes but not in athletes. Which reading is most careful?

options.text: Athletes may have less room to gain, and only four athlete studies exist
options.why: Right: athletes sit close to their ceiling, and the athlete estimate (−1.07, CI −3.51 to 1.37) rests on four studies, so it is imprecise.

options.text: It proves hypoxia harms the VO2max of athletes
options.why: The CI includes zero and positive values, so harm is not shown.

options.text: It proves non-athletes respond for biological reasons alone
options.why: Non-athletes may also be more prone to placebo effects, since few studies blinded them; the authors raise this.

options.text: It shows VO2max cannot be trained in athletes
options.why: LHTL did raise it in athletes, by about 2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: What most limits how far to trust the live-high train-low result in the 2026 meta-analysis?

options.text: Few studies blinded participants, so placebo effects may inflate gains
options.why: Right: none of the 10 LHTL studies blinded participants, most studies had some concerns or high risk of bias, and the authors say placebo effects are likely.

options.text: A funnel plot and the Egger test showed strong publication bias
options.why: The Egger test was not significant (p = 0.67) and the funnel plot looked symmetric.

options.text: The review was paid for by a company selling altitude tents
options.why: The authors declared no specific funding and no conflicts of interest.

options.text: The review included animal studies as well as human ones
options.why: It included controlled studies in healthy humans.

variants.stem: The meta-analysis pools studies of VO2max. Why is a higher VO2max after live-high train-low not the same as a faster race?

options.text: VO2max is one factor; economy, threshold and pacing also decide results
options.why: Right: the review measured VO2max only, and the authors note that sport performance can differ from it.

options.text: VO2max is fixed by genes, so measured changes are only noise
options.why: VO2max does respond to training; the issue is that it is only one determinant of race results.

options.text: VO2max is measured in different units in every study
options.why: The authors report results as mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; units are not the problem.

options.text: A lab VO2max test is too unreliable to detect any change at all
options.why: Test noise widens confidence intervals, but the LHTL gain in athletes was clear of zero; the issue is that VO2max is one factor.
